title: Long-Term Thinking For A Short-Sighted World

questions.q: What does the Mayan calendar example illustrate?
a: The Mayans thought on a far longer timescale than we do
The world narrowly avoided ending in 2012
Ancient calendars were less accurate than modern ones
Every calendar eventually resets after 5,129 years
questions.why: The overview uses the calendar rollover to contrast Mayan long-term thinking with our own short-term habits.

questions.q: How does living by the clock affect our thinking?
a: It strengthens our tendency toward short-term decisions
It makes us better at planning decades ahead
It removes our awareness that time is passing
It slows our reactions to sudden change
questions.why: The first lesson says modern life in 5, 10 and 25 minute intervals trains us to expect immediate results.

questions.q: What was the core problem with the rise of cars?
a: Nobody considered their long-term environmental impact
They were too expensive for most families to buy
They replaced a public transport system that worked well
They caused the world's oil supply to run out quickly
questions.why: The second lesson says cars were instantly popular, but their environmental impact was devastating because no one thought long term.

questions.q: Why does the summary recommend spending money at local businesses?
a: They reinvest more locally and have a long-term stake in the community
Local goods are always cheaper than imported products
Local shops create more jobs than large factories do
Local products are reliably of higher quality
questions.why: The third lesson says local businesses cannot simply move away, so they have a lasting interest in the community's well-being.

questions.q: How much of each dollar spent at a local business is reinvested locally?
a: 55 cents
15 cents
30 cents
75 cents
questions.why: The summary contrasts local businesses, which reinvest 55 cents of every dollar, with big brands at only 15 cents.
